description: A duo-driven project focused on decoding the mysteries of the outer solar system. Our mission for this hackathon is to explore the "Planet X" challenge by combining scientific curiosity with interactive digital solutions, proving that a single passionate mind can contribute to big space concepts.
summary: SkyShift is a free web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx all-sky infrared images into a time-lapse of any spot on the sky. Type a star name or coordinates, and SkyShift asks the IRSA archive which SPHEREx exposures cover that position, streams only the needed pixel rows from NASA's public cloud archive, aligns and stacks them by epoch, and plays them as a blinking movie, so anything that moves or changes brightness stands out. Because every SPHEREx exposure sees a slightly different infrared colour, SkyShift also rebuilds a 0.75–5 µm spectrum on the fly, measures brightness changes over time, fits proper motion with sub-pixel precision, and scans the whole field for unknown moving sources. We validated it on the challenge targets: Barnard's Star (measured 10.25″/yr vs 10.39″/yr catalogue), WISE 0855, ε Indi B, and the variables RW Aurigae and R Draconis. Everything runs in the browser with no install, and new SPHEREx data releases appear automatically.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SkyShift lets anyone explore how the sky changes in NASA SPHEREx data. The user enters a name or coordinates (or clicks a featured target) and sees six-month epochs blink like a movie. Five display modes help the eye: Blink, Difference (each epoch minus all others, so movers appear as red/blue pairs), Colour = time (still stars are white, movers leave a rainbow trail), Infrared colour (the six detectors combined into RGB, so cold brown dwarfs glow red) and single Exposures with contamination flags. Clicking any star shows its 0.75–5 µm spectrum built on the fly with molecule markers (H₂O, CH₄, CO, CO₂), its brightness history, and its measured motion. A Mover Scan tracks every source in the field and flags the ones that move. Coordinates can be put in the URL, so any view can be shared or embedded.

HOW IT WORKS

1. The browser asks the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive (TAP service) which SPHEREx exposures cover the position, through a tiny read-only proxy, because the archive does not allow direct browser requests.

2. Instead of downloading 66 MB FITS files, SkyShift reads only the needed pixel rows (about 0.4 MB) from NASA's public SPHEREx bucket on AWS using HTTP Range requests.

3. A FITS reader and the TAN-SIP coordinate system written in JavaScript (checked against astropy) place every exposure on a common north-up grid.

4. Exposures are stacked per epoch with outlier rejection. We found that about 0.7% of pixels in each exposure are hot pixels or cosmic rays, which otherwise create fake "moving objects".

5. SPHEREx's linear variable filters mean each exposure sees a different wavelength, read from the WCS-WAVE table. Measuring the target in all exposures gives its spectrum, and dividing by that spectrum gives a clean light curve.

6. Motion is measured with centroids or a joint PSF fit (needed for WISE 0855, which sits 6″ from a background star), corrected with field stars. Saturated stars like R Draconis are measured from their PSF wings.

VALIDATION ON THE CHALLENGE TARGETS

Barnard's Star: −0.76/+10.22 ″/yr (catalogue −0.80/+10.36). WISE 0855: −7.85/−0.21 ″/yr (catalogue −8.12/+0.67), invisible below 4 µm and bright at 4–5 µm, exactly as a very cold brown dwarf should be. ε Indi B: +3.54/−2.70 ″/yr (catalogue +3.97/−2.54), found blind by Mover Scan. RW Aurigae: no motion, about 9% brightness change. R Draconis: about 59% brightness change between epochs (Mira variable).

IMPACT

Most comets and brown dwarfs were found by volunteers comparing images. SkyShift brings SPHEREx's 102-colour view to anyone with a browser, with no install, no account and no astronomy software, and adds measurements (spectra, motion, variability) that usually need specialist tools. It always queries all data releases, and a weekly automatic update keeps the featured targets current as new SPHEREx data arrive.

TOOLS

Plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS (no framework), Node.js (local server and scripts), Cloudflare Worker (proxy), GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions (hosting and weekly data refresh), IndexedDB (browser cache), Aladin Lite (sky map). The code and documentation were developed with the help of an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic); the team designed the approach, tested and debugged the tool on the challenge targets and validated the results against published catalogues. Our full development diary is in DEVLOG.md in the repository.

LIMITATIONS

Fluxes are approximate in absolute terms (no aperture correction) but reliable for colours, spectral shapes and changes. Parallax needs more epochs than exist today.
